The mixed slurry was uniformly spread on a thin aluminum foil with a thickness of 15 -m, followed by drying at $8 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ for 1 h. The electrodes were cut into $2 \times 2$ cm pieces and then roll-pressed to increase the number of inter-particle contacts. The pressed electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 80◦C for 12 h. Half-cells were then assembled with the bare or $Z _ { \mathrm { { I n O } } } .$ -coated $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ as the working electrode, lithium metal foil as the counter electrode, 1 M $_ { \mathrm { L i P F } _ { 6 } - \mathrm { E C } : \mathrm { D M C } : \mathrm { E M C } }$ (1:1:1 by volume) as the electrolyte, and a polypropylene-based film as the separator. Fig. 5(a) shows the changes in the discharge capacities during repeated charge-discharge cycling for the bare and ZnO-coated LiCoO with different coating amounts. The ZnO coating substantially improves the cyclic performance of $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ . The results of the cycling test in the range of $3 . 0 { - } 4 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V }$ reveal that both bare and ZnO-coated $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ materials exhibit little difference in their discharge capacity during the first few cycles. In subsequent cycles, however, the bare $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ abruptly degrades, whereas the ZnO-coated $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ fades relatively slowly. In addition, different coating amounts cause different degrees of capacity retention upon cycling. Fig. 5(b) shows the capacity retention of the test cells after 30 cycles as a function of the concentration of deposited $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , where capacity retention is defined as the percentage of the discharge capacity that remains after the 30th cycle with respect to the discharge capacity at the first cycle. Compared with bare LiCoO that displays a capacity retention of 37% after 30 cycles, the 0.21 wt.% ZnO-coated $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ retained approximately 65% of its initial capacity. Further increases in the coating amount result in a decrease in cyclic stability, which might be due in part to the electrochemical inactivity resulting from the excess coating materials. It is believed that the presence of an excess amount of ZnO on the surface of the matrix particles may lead to a decrease in the particle–particle electronic conductivity and the formation of agglomerated ZnO particles, as observed on the surface of0.49 wt.% $\mathsf { Z n O - L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ . This may inhibit lithium-ion transport through the interface between the surface layer and cathode particles.

33: Cobalt dissolution from a $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ cathode during high-voltage cycling, which causes degradation ofthe $\mathrm { L i C o O _ { 2 } }$ structure, is widely held to be one of the major reasons for capacity fading at high cutoff voltages [17–20]. For a direct examination of the effect of the surface coating on Co dissolution from $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ cathode, approximately 70 mg ofthe bare and 0.21 wt.% ZnO-coated $\mathrm { i } { \mathsf { C o O } } _ { 2 }$ powders, which were used in the cycling test (30 cycles at 1 C rate), were prepared and then immersed in a 1 M LiPF -EC:DMC:EMC(1:1:1 by volume) electrolyte for 10 days at 80◦C. As shown in Table 2, the amount of Co dissolved from the 0.21 wt.% ZnO-coated LiCoO is less than 0.1 ppm, which is much lower than that from the bare $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 } ,$ viz., 0.79 ppm. This indicates that the uniform dispersion of ZnO nanoparticles on the $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ surface can effectively reduce the contact area between the $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ and electrolyte which, in turn, can reduce the dissolution of Co ions from $\mathrm { L i C o O } _ { 2 }$ into the electrolyte.
